49163955-f335-5ec9-ad16-f40d332e867a.name: *The Beheading of St. Paul*
49163955-f335-5ec9-ad16-f40d332e867a.description:
*The Beheading of St. Paul* was commissioned by Virgilio Spada to a Bolognese sculptor, living in Rome, Alessandro Algardi. The statues were made in Rome and shipped to Bologna. They were intended to decorate the high altar of the Barnabite Church San Paolo Maggiore – St. Paul’s, patronised by the Spada family and to commemorate Virgilio’s father, Paul. Upon his death, in 1631, 6000 scudi was bequeathed for the construction of a chapel. In 1634 the Spada moved their residence from Rome to Bologna and Virgilio obtained permission from the pope for building the family chapel in Bologna, instead of Rome. After a few months the Spada made an agreement with the Barnabite fathers in Bologna. They were allowed to build the façade of the church and the high altar with its marble group and shrine. Gian Lorenzo Bernini designed the projects for the shrine and the group was commissioned in 1634 to Alessandro Algardi. The altar was officially inaugurated in 1647. In 1648 Virgilio Spada commissioned a bronze bas-relief to Algardi for the frontal of the same altar, depicting the beheading of St. Paul.  
This beautiful group shows the executioner prepared to cut St. Paul’s head with his sword. The saint looks down and offers his head to the blow. There is a strong contrast between the movement of the executioner’s body and the static attitude of the saint. The bas-relief shows what followed after the execution according to tradition: the saint’s head bounces three times on the ground and creates three springs.
49163955-f335-5ec9-ad16-f40d332e867a.short_description: The group depicts the moment of the beheading of St Paul. Typically, baroque is the juxtaposition between the Saint, already part a heavenly atmosphere, and the executioner with his cruel grimace. The artist succeeds in conveying the tension preceding the blow and the contrast between the saint’s serenity and the executioner’s tense mobility. The beautiful shrine framing the group creates a link with the architecture of the interior of the church.

493e7023-35e9-59c4-960b-226c4901faf1.name: *Model for the Equestrian Sculpture of King Louis XIV*
493e7023-35e9-59c4-960b-226c4901faf1.description:
The terracotta model for the equestrian monument to Louis XIV was created by Bernini, already in his seventies, in late 1669 and 1670. The sculpture of the Sun King on horseback was ordered during a trip to Paris by Bernini in 1665, but we know from a letter sent by the artist to Minister Colbert, that it was not confirmed until 1669. The sculptor, who had studied his model carefully in Paris, decided to show him on the Mount of Glory controlling his galloping horse, his sceptre held horizontally; a symbol of regal equity. Although Bernini was not aware of the location intended for the sculpture, he arranged it – in accordance with Baroque taste – favouring a particular view point, in this case from the left, like the contemporary numismatics showing the king on horseback. This work can be traced back to several models both in ancient sculpture and modern painting and sculpture, most notably the model for the equestrian monument of Francis I by Leonardo (Budapest, Szépmuűvészeti Múzeum).  
The sculpture was transported to France in 1685, some years after Bernini's death and, as it did not please the king, it was then moved to Versailles. The work was transformed into Marcus Curtius by the French sculptor François Girardon and placed in a hidden corner of the gardens. The execution of the sculpture is actually quite ordinary: it was done by pupils of the French Academy in Rome and not directly by the artist and his prestigious Roman workshop. This makes the autography of this terracotta model of paramount importance, its bursting vitality reviving the splendour of the Berninian idea and his creative journey.  
The work was sold several times before ending up in the Contini Bonacossi Collection, from where it was given to the Galleria Borghese in 1923, a donation that was made permanent in 1926.
493e7023-35e9-59c4-960b-226c4901faf1.short_description: This terracotta was modelled by Bernini in Rome for an equestrian monument of Louis XIV, but the sculpture itself was executed by his pupils. The king, however, did not appreciate the work, and so it was transformed into Marcus Curtius by the French sculptor Francois Girardon, and transferred to Versailles (now at the Louvre).
493e7023-35e9-59c4-960b-226c4901faf1.obtention: Donated to the Italian state by the Contini Bonacossi family in 1926.

499f5994-2858-5519-8d58-193c2a6b45ee.name: *Jupiter and Semele*
499f5994-2858-5519-8d58-193c2a6b45ee.description:
A diagonal composition of a pair of nudes in dramatic poses, the picture conveys a story from Greek mythology retold by Ovid in the third volume of *Metamorphoses*. Semele, daughter of Cadmus, the founder of Thebes, tricked by jealous Hera who wants to spoil Zeus's (Jupiter's) philandering, gets Jupiter to grant her wish that he should visit her in his true shape. Saddened, Zeus takes on his divine form, summoning clouds, rain, storm and gale, thunderbolts and lightning. Mortal Semele cannot withstand the raging elements and perishes. Her son Bacchus (Dionysus), conceived earlier, survives, as Zeus sews him into his thigh and carries the future god of wine to full term himself.  
From late renaissance onwards, Ovid's texts were recommended to artists as a wellspring of subjects and were published in a number of illustrated editions. Themes derived from mythology frequently decorated studies and whole mansions. The most popular included erotic scenes, particularly Zeus (Jupiter) visiting his lovers in various shapes, transformed into animals, elements or simple mortals.  
The painted frame of the picture suggests that the canvas was part of an interior decoration, the location for which is as yet unknown. The colour scheme, based on contrasts between blue and red, illuminated by the scale of light, and the peachy tones used for the anatomically elaborate nudes, also has a decorative nature. In addition, it underlines the psychological effect of the bodies portrayed. The discovery of two preparatory sketches in the collection of the State Science Library, Olomouc, allows speculation as to Moravian provenance for the picture. During the period 1691–95 Pagani worked in Kroměříž, Mikulov and on the Velehrad basilica. He probably left for Cracow with the B. Fontana workshop and returned to Italy via Olomouc.
499f5994-2858-5519-8d58-193c2a6b45ee.short_description: The decorative composition of a pair of nudes in dramatic poses conveys a story from Greek mythology retold by Ovid in the third volume of *Metamorphoses*. The painted frame of the picture suggests that the canvas was part of an interior decoration, the location for which is as yet unknown.
499f5994-2858-5519-8d58-193c2a6b45ee.obtention: The picture was purchased by the Provincial Committee from the Spielmann Collection, Berlin, in 1931.

4c3f617a-7e2c-59e0-b879-f12b80b2aac8.name: *Allegory of Autumn*
4c3f617a-7e2c-59e0-b879-f12b80b2aac8.description: This painting is part of a series representing the *Four Seasons*. It was painted by Pier Francesco Cittadini, a Milanese artist who was a follower of Guido Reni of Bologna. The cycle is described by the eighteenth-century art historian Luigi Crespi in his book *Felsina Pittrice*, printed in 1769. At that time, it was the property of a noble Bolognese family, the Counts Legnani. *Spring* and *Summer* are today housed in the Galleria Estense in Modena; *Winter* and *Autumn* hang together in the same room in the Collezioni Comunali d'Arte in Bologna. Wreaths of fruit and vegetables frame landscapes with mythological scenes connected with the seasons. *Autumn* is symbolised by Bacchus with a vine wreath on his head and a thyrsus in his hand. On the right a drunken Silenus lays down next to a vat. Vine-shoots, pumpkins and pomegranates frame the scene. Cittadini learned this kind of composition, a mixture of still life, mythological scenes and landscape, typical of Flemish painters, during his stay in Rome.
4c3f617a-7e2c-59e0-b879-f12b80b2aac8.short_description: This painting is part of a series depicting the *Four Seasons* painted for the Counts Legnani of Bologna. It is the work of Pier Francesco Cittadini, a Milanese painter celebrated for his still lives and portraits. Bacchus, supervising the wine-making process personifies the allegory of Autumn; a wreath of seasonal fruit, following the Flemish tradition, frames the scene.
4c3f617a-7e2c-59e0-b879-f12b80b2aac8.method_for_datation: The series of the *Four Seasons* is generally connected for stylistic reasons with the garlands of flowers and fruit painted by Cittadini for the Ducal palace in Sassuolo (Gallery of Bacchus), a summer residence of the Este family, where he worked from 1650.
4c3f617a-7e2c-59e0-b879-f12b80b2aac8.obtention: This painting together with its pendant, *Winter*, entered the municipal collections in 1930, through the bequest of Marquis Pier Ignazio Rusconi.

4de3eb32-b57d-5953-83b6-9b88acb3de21.name: *St. Francis Xavier*
4de3eb32-b57d-5953-83b6-9b88acb3de21.description:
Following liberation from Turkish occupation, the Jesuits were among the first to occupy the prominent towns of northeast Croatia. They arrived in Požega, a town at the very heart of the so-called *Valis Aurea*, the Golden Valley surrounded by mountains, in the middle of the Slavonian plain.  
This painting of St. Francis Xavier was probably among the first artworks installed to decorate the Jesuit College in Požega, built and equipped soon after the Jesuit's arrival in 1698. The pendant to this painting presents the Immaculate Conception in a very specific way, with the Madonna sitting on a throne and the Child standing on a serpent's head next to her.  
*St. Francis Xavier* shows the saint baptising the local inhabitants on one of his missions to the East. The composition is common in works with a similar theme, for example, in the small-size oil painting, the *Baptism of Queen Neachila of India* by the same artist. This work, a kind of study or *bozzetto*, is in Düsseldorf Museum, while a painting of the same subject on a larger scale is in the Kiscelli Museum, Budapest.  
In the Požega painting, the figure of the saint is notable for its monumental gesture: the almost three-quarter length, front-facing figure of the saint pouring holy water from the small bucket onto the heads of the three figures gathered around the baptismal font. The stunning texture of the paint reveals the author's dynamic gestural brushstrokes. The somewhat cold and distant colours are surprising in a scene supposedly taking place in Asia and Africa, where warmer and more saturated colours are expected. Nevertheless, the specific chromatic values seen here are frequent in Pozzo's paintings, as are the dynamic brushstrokes.
4de3eb32-b57d-5953-83b6-9b88acb3de21.short_description: *St. Francis Xavier* is one of a few easel paintings by the Baroque painter, architect and art theoretician Andrea Pozzo. Brought to Požega by the Jesuits soon after 1698 after liberation from the Ottomans, the stunning detail reveals the author's eloquent gestural brushstrokes.
4de3eb32-b57d-5953-83b6-9b88acb3de21.holder: Diocese Museum of the Požega Diocese
4de3eb32-b57d-5953-83b6-9b88acb3de21.method_for_datation: The date and the origin of this painting were established partly by the *Historia domus* of the Jesuit College in Požega and through comparative analysis of other known works by the same author.
4de3eb32-b57d-5953-83b6-9b88acb3de21.obtention: Originally owned by the Jesuits of Požega, Joseph II confiscated this painting along with the entire Jesuit inventory when he banned the order. Some of the paintings became part of the Diocese Museum of the Zagreb Archdiocese. Shortly after the Požega Diocese was established, the painting was returned to Požega.

4f168169-4f01-599e-9115-78ac90105ab9.name: Jesuit Church of St Ignatius, college and Jesuit stairs, Dubrovnik
4f168169-4f01-599e-9115-78ac90105ab9.description:
Dedicated to the founder of the Society, St. Ignatius, the Jesuit Church of St Ignatius in Dubrovnik draws on the monumental prototype of Il Gesù, the Jesuit church in Rome. However, Andrea Pozzo, to encapsulate the stylistic sensibilities of the High Baroque, transformed this Early Baroque prototype. As with most of Pozzo's architecture (for example, the Jesuit Church of St. Ignatius, Rome) the Church of St Ignatius, Dubrovnik, is a nave, barrel-vaulted church, lit by a basilica, and with side chapels and lofts. The uniform rhythm of the spatial units is enlivened, however, with the alternation of broad bays with chapels and narrow bays with galleries (separated from each other with Corinthian pilasters). The central bay is emphasised by the transversal axis of the side entrances. The dominant longitudinal axis culminates (as in Pozzo's reworking of the Jesuit church in Vienna) in scenic treatment of the sanctuary; powerful in its plastic articulation and rich in wall paintings.  
A similar High Baroque aesthetic characterises the facade of the church: a dynamic central zone with freestanding pillars and a monumental portal decorated with sculptural angels, by the Venetian sculptor and architect, Marino Gropelli.  
The low entry-wing of the college, from which the concluding façade of the high side-wing continues, creates an undulating, theatrical backdrop to the square below and, overall, a graceful whole is achieved in the church's elevation. Sculptures by Pietro Passalacqua enrich the traditional interior of the four-winged college, divided into internal corridors and external sequences of rooms. Passalacqua's main contribution is, however, the monumental Jesuit stairway, designed according to the well-known Spanish Steps in Rome (also Late Baroque).
4f168169-4f01-599e-9115-78ac90105ab9.short_description: The Jesuit complex with its college, church and approach staircase is a unique production of Baroque architecture and town planning in Croatia. Founded from the bequest of Dubrovnik Jesuit, Marin Gundulić, it was created over a period in excess of 100 years (1653–1765). Built according to the designs of several architects, two of whom – Andrea Pozzo and Pietro Passalacqua – belong at the highest level in European architecture, its construction charts a sequence of stylistic constructions. The complex has Early Baroque characteristics in the four-winged ground plan of the college; the High Baroque is seen in the spatial organisation and paintings of the nave church with its side chapels and, finally, the Late Baroque is seen in the dynamic and scenic conception of the approach stairway.
4f168169-4f01-599e-9115-78ac90105ab9.type: Religious architecture, a High Baroque longitudinal nave church with side chapels and lofts, a Baroque four-winged college and Late Baroque city staircase
4f168169-4f01-599e-9115-78ac90105ab9.dates: Church (1699–1725); college (second half of the 17th and first half of the 18th century); stairs (1738)
4f168169-4f01-599e-9115-78ac90105ab9.method_for_datation: On the basis of documents, archival plans and stylistic features.

Marković, V., “Pietro Passalacqua u Dubrovniku” in *Peristil* 24, 1981, pp. 95–114.

4f168169-4f01-599e-9115-78ac90105ab9.history:
Pronounced Baroque features are in evidence in the very location of this Jesuit complex. Situated in a dominant position in the oldest, southern part of the city there was particular investment to ensure its position, seen in the extant plan of the first rector, Gianbattisto Canauli (1653), which shows that through purchases and demolition of houses an entire neighbourhood was redeveloped and rebuilt.  
Construction started in 1662, under the eye of Jesuit Serafino Fabrini from Rome. The original design included a four-winged and, in addition, a polygonal church. The 1667 earthquake halted building of this exceptional rotunda – similar to that of St. Vitus (Vid) in Rijeka, however. The earthquake, apart from temporarily stopping construction, also resulted in the territorial expansion of the complex – thus making possible the construction of a longitudinal church more suitable to the needs of the Jesuits (1699–1725) – after a design by the leading Jesuit architect and painter, Andrea Pozzo of Trent. The final phase and peak of building development of the Jesuit complex was marked by the construction of a monumental stone stairway (1738), the work of  a Roman architect of Sicilian descent, Pietro Passalacqua, which linked the square in front of the college and church with the town centre.
4f168169-4f01-599e-9115-78ac90105ab9.architects: Architect of the first college and the central church ( not built): Serafino Fabrini (active 1661–1662); designer of the longitudinal Church of St. Ignatius: Andrea Pozzo (1699–1725); sculptures on the facade of the church: Marino Gropelli (1662–1728); wall paintings in the sanctuary of the church: Gaetano Garcia (active 1735–1738); renovation of the college and architect of the Jesuit stairs: Pietro Passalacqua (1690–1748)

55911031-be2b-569a-a628-497ca9a99626.name: Church of St. George in Purga Lepoglavska
55911031-be2b-569a-a628-497ca9a99626.alternate_name: Kapela sv. Jurja u Purgi Lepoglavskoj
55911031-be2b-569a-a628-497ca9a99626.description:
The ceiling paintings in the Church of St. George are Ivan Krstitelj Ranger's most mature work. The carefully designed *quadratura* give the illusion that the modest architectural space of the church is larger and lighter than it really is. The iconographical framework of the chapel is the Life and Death of St. George, one of north Croatia's most popular patron saints. Other saints furnish the painted side altars in illusionistic niches: on the left that dedicated to Saint Mary of the Sorrows and, on the right, *St. Anthony of Padua*, *St. Barbara*, *St. Apollonia* and *Judas Maccabeus*. On the walls are emblems and other symbols and an allegory of spring beneath showing a church chorus; angels in concert – everything speaks in favour of a more complex meaning to be seen in the entirety.  
The famous scene of the furious fight between St. George and the dragon plays out on a painted stage on the wall of the apse. While they are placed in the interior, the princess in distress is waiting and praying in the landscape “outside” the church, which we can seen behind the baluster fence painted in the middle of the wall. The theatrical illusion is upheld by the presence of a Pauline monk and a middle-aged man in a theatre box on the upper left-hand side of the presbytery. The most important “audience” is, however, the one painted on the ceiling vault: God the Father, Christ and angels holding symbols of heavenly glory and martyrdom. The *quadratura* of the church culminates in the illusionist dome painted above the only nave.
55911031-be2b-569a-a628-497ca9a99626.short_description: There are few churches as small as this one dedicated to St. George in Purga Lepoglavska, not far from the Pauline monastery in Lepoglava where the extraordinarily talented illusionistic painter, Ivan Krstitelj Ranger, was a lay-brother painter. Ranger was born in north Tyrol but left no works in his home country. Instead, he arrived in Lepoglava and settled in the Pauline monastery. All Ranger's known works, with the exception of the ceiling paintings in Olimlje in nearby Slovenia, were commissions in north Croatia. The ceiling paintings in the Church of St. George are Ranger's most mature work with carefully designed *quadratura* thatgive the illusion extend the modest architectural space of the church.

The modest architectural frame of the chapel was complete by 1749, and soon after in 1750, Ivan Krstitelj Ranger accomplished the illusionist paintings.

55ee9fa2-41da-5e33-bce1-dc44c9ed3296.name: Slavonski Brod Fortress
55ee9fa2-41da-5e33-bce1-dc44c9ed3296.description:
Constructed under Prince Eugene of Savoy as Chairman of the Court Council of War, Slavonski Brod Fortress belongs to the west wing of a large system of Baroque fortress-towns constructed at the Danube node on the border with the Turkish empire. Although the system represents the central and most interesting chapter in the development of fortification architecture and urbanism of Baroque fortress towns in the first half of the 18th century, it has to date been insufficiently studied. Construction works by Prince Eugene of Savoy for his own purposes hold a high position in the history of architecture. Through his construction activities, Prince Eugene of Savoy intended to retain the acquired power of the Empire, and although the Prince contributed much to the architectural heritage of the period, his contribution remained hidden to his biographers despite numerous documents – particularly plans and project notes for fortress-towns – kept in Vienna and a number of other European archives.  
Slavonski Brod Fortress, constructed on the banks of the River Sava a key crossing towards Bosnia, is unique in that it was an independent fortress constructed and connected to an existing settlement. In contrast, Osijek and Petrovaradin (as well as later fortress-towns such as Temeswar, Belgrade and Carlsburg constructed to further strengthen the defence system), were existing urban structures that were transformed into Baroque fortress-towns through the construction of fortifications and radical transformation.
55ee9fa2-41da-5e33-bce1-dc44c9ed3296.short_description: The fortress, constructed between 1691 and 1731, was one of the fortress-towns built under the leadership of Prince Eugen of Savoy. According to recent research, the octagonal church of St. Anne erected in the central square in 1743, belonged to a characteristic type developed by Johann Lucas von Hildebrandt.
55ee9fa2-41da-5e33-bce1-dc44c9ed3296.bibliography: Uzelac, Z., “The Church of St Anne of Brod Fort in Slavonski Brod – a work of Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt of 1743” in *Radovi institute za povijest umjetnosti* 28, 2004, pp. 188–207.
55ee9fa2-41da-5e33-bce1-dc44c9ed3296.history: According to plans adopted in 1715, the fortress seemed to take the form of fortresses from an earlier period initially, differing from them only in size. The large size was the result of adopting the quadrant-style of the existing settlement. This originally square fortress was modernised in 1729 by the Swiss architect, Nicolaus Doxat de Demoret the main architect of all Border towns including Vauban in Austria, who transformed it into an impressive star-shaped fortress. After defeat by Turkey (1737–1739), the death of Emperor Charles VI and the subsequent change in historical circumstances during the early reign of Empress Maria Theresia, the military border became the main residence of army personnel in preparation for the battlefield. The military commander of Slavonia, General Ascanio de Guadagni – a Florentine in the Imperial service and later Marshall and Governor of Tyrol – muted his proposals for the construction of a church at Slavonski Brod in 1739. On his initiative, in 1742, the Court Council of War decided to construct a Military Church at Slavonski Brod.
keywords: Military urbanism, fortress, Slavonski Brod, church, Johann Lucas von Hildebrandt

5647174a-d70c-5acf-8ebd-27ca4e8179a6.name: *St. Barbara*
5647174a-d70c-5acf-8ebd-27ca4e8179a6.description:
This half-figure of a woman holding a palm frond suggests a Christian martyr; the chalice, communion wafer, sword and tower in the background help identify her as St. Barbara, the patron saint of miners, artillerymen, gunsmiths and all who work with explosives. Legend has it that her father, a pagan nobleman, had a tower erected to imprison his daughter and discourage prospective suitors. The tower had only two windows. In her father’s absence, Barbara persuaded workers to add a third window. She also had a priest visit in secret and baptise her. When her father returned, Barbara explained that the three windows symbolised the Holy Trinity illuminating her soul. The father turned her over to the Roman authorities. When Barbara refused to abandon her faith, she was tortured and finally decapitated.  
The monochrome colour scheme, light contrasts and the artist’s original handwriting hint at inspiration by Dutch and Flemish 17th-century painting. The smoothly arched face contrasts with the relaxed rendering of the drapery. The portrait features of the saint suggest an interest in individual psychology, and embody a crypto-portrait of the artist’s wife.  
Willmann was probably apprenticed to his father’s workshop before leaving for the Netherlands. It has been maintained that he was a direct student of Rembrandt; he certainly came into contact with Rembrandt’s art and was allegedly in touch with Jacob de Backer, a student of Rembrandt, as well as with a circle of landscape artists around Jacob van Ruisdael. In Antwerp, he became acquainted with the work of Rubens and Van Dyck. The painter later moved to Breslau where his work attracted the interest of the Cistercian abbot of the Lubiaz monastery. The artist joined his service and settled in Lubiaz for good, painting for the abbey and other monasteries in Bohemia and Moravia. His stay was only broken by a trip to the Elector’s court in Berlin, where he was appointed court painter.

The smoothly arched face contrasts with the relaxed rendering of the drapery. The portrait features of the saint embody a crypto-portrait of the artist’s wife.

5e0ab537-5406-5e3a-b38e-c14b779c789f.name: Sant'Agostino in San Michele
5e0ab537-5406-5e3a-b38e-c14b779c789f.description: The church has a simple slender gabled façade with side capitals holding a frieze framing the central window. There is only a portal. The wall still bears signs of the older structure including a gable frieze and a closed arch which is part of a portico once standing at the side of the portal. The church has one nave with three chapels on each side. Each chapel is framed by columns with Corinthians capitals and between the columns are wooden confessional boxes. Above each confessional opens a niche hosting allegorical figures (*Mercy*, *Charity*, *Justice*, *Humility*, *Penitence*, and *Wisdom*) moulded in stucco. *St. Michael Defeating the Devil* is made of the same material. All the sculptures are works of the Bolognese sculptor Angelo Gabriello Piò (1690–1770), who was aided by his son Domenico. He often collaborated with architects like Dotti, Ambrosi and Viaggi, because of his skill in mixing sculptural decoration and architecture. We have no documentary evidence but Piò was probably summoned to Imola to work in Sant'Agostino about 1750.
5e0ab537-5406-5e3a-b38e-c14b779c789f.short_description: The façade of the church bears many traces of its older history: the rose window and the corbel freeze go back to the twelve-century. In 1354 the church passed to the Augustinan Fathers who started a complete remodelling. Further enlargements followed in the fourteenth and sixteenth centuries, leading to the present building. The stucco decoration inside the church was moulded by the Bolognese sculptor Angelo Gabriello Piò who made it about 1750. Piò worked in strict contact with Domenico Morelli, the Ticinese architect who rebuilt the church starting from 1747.

5e0ab537-5406-5e3a-b38e-c14b779c789f.history:
The church of Sant'Agostino flanks the via Emilia and opens on the via Marsala. The original church was built in the mid fourteenth-century. The Augustinian fathers, living outside Porta Piolo decided to relocate to inside the town walls. They moved into an already extant church, the Romanesque San Michele documented from the twelve-century. Preserving the former name in the parish church intitulation, they decided to rebuild it. The building was enlarged in the fourteenth-and fifteenth-centuries. The present church was remodelled by two architects, Domenico and Cosimo Morelli from Ticino and working in the Legazione Pontificia. Domenico, father of Cosimo, planned the structure of the church starting from 1747, as shown in the original documents. In 1767 his son changed the presbiterium and the apsis, partially changing his father's design. Construction ended in 1769. Cosimo Morelli worked alongside his brother Luigi and the masters Trifogli and Diabene, a sign of the well-organised équipe work in Ticinese workshops.  
On the counter façade, above the main door, stands a group with the *Archangel Michael Defeating the Devil*. On the sides, between columns, are the statues of *Mercy*, *Charity*, *Justice*, *Humility*, *Penitence*, *Wisdom*.  
In 1798 the parish church of Sant'Agostino became subsidiary; It was reopened in 1826 as parish church.
5e0ab537-5406-5e3a-b38e-c14b779c789f.architects:
Architects: Domenico Morelli and Cosimo Morelli (1732–1812); sculptors: Angelo Gabriello (1690–1770) and Domenico Piò (1715–1801).  
Angelo Piò started as a pupil of the Ferrarese Andrea Ferreri. In 1712 he entered the workshop of Giuseppe Maria Mazza, who changed the sculptural language of Bologna in the second half of the seventeenth-century. He worked with Camillo Rusconi in Rome. Upon returning to Bologna he became a member of the local Accademia Clementina. He worked intensely and exclusively for Bologna and its province beginning in the thirties.

691f4869-9119-56f3-80c5-8cdfac543dce.name: Liechtenstein Residence, Valtice
691f4869-9119-56f3-80c5-8cdfac543dce.description: The original seat, a medieval castle, became part of a new palace in the 17th century, fulfilling a memorial function by demonstrating the ancient nature of the family. The “heart“ of the residence, the *studiolo*, a room for contemplation with exempla and patterns of debates, housed a ducal crown with a diamond, an allusion to the family name, literally “stone of light”. The demolition of this section in around 1744, and a reconstruction by A. E. Martinelli, completed the restoration of the chateau.
691f4869-9119-56f3-80c5-8cdfac543dce.short_description: The chateau, outbuildings and park, once the seat of the most powerful aristocratic family in Moravia, make up monument listed as a UNESCO World Cultural Heritage site. The count’s residence was the centre of culture and economic administration for a large demesne in Valtice. The early Baroque was first introduced to Central Europe by Italian artists, with masters from Vienna taking part in later phases. The design of the residence follows a “triumphal path” schema. The chateau, the church and the town with a monastery hospital, make up a single whole, demonstrating the history, glory and power of the Liechtenstein family.
691f4869-9119-56f3-80c5-8cdfac543dce.method_for_datation: Records in accounts and contracts for individual commissions for the construction of the residence have been preserved. On the basis of these, and with the help of old pictures of the chateau, it is possible to trace, at least partially, its original state. Beduzzi’s architectural drawings are held in the Moravian Gallery in Brno.

691f4869-9119-56f3-80c5-8cdfac543dce.history: Valtice is among the oldest settlements in the country. The castle dating from 1193 belonged to the Bishop of Passau. The Liechtensteins acquired the property in 1395. Karel of Liechtenstein converted to Catholicism before the Battle of White Mountain and became the governor of the Czech kingdom, securing important positions for his descendants. The family property equalled the property of the Church and amounted to some 20 per cent of the country’s gross national product. In the early 18th century, the Schellenberg and Vaduz demesnes were affiliated to the Moravian property; since 1945 Vaduz has been the home of the Liechtenstein family, with its roots reaching back to the 12th century. Its network of residences throughout Moravia, Austria and Liechtenstein included buildings of different types and functions, manifesting the family status. The town is a centre of Moravian viticulture: the Cellar of the Cross (1640) is one of the largest in the Czech lands.

6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.name: *St. John the Evangelist*
6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.description:
St. John the Evangelist, gospel author and apocalyptic visionary, holds the Book of Revelations, with seals. At his feet is an eagle, one of his attributes. The eagle's mighty flight and the ancient belief that the bird could shade (or stop) the sun contributed to its coming to symbolise the soul and a mystic vision of God. Much of the animal symbolism of the Evangelists is derived from the Old Testament vision of Ezekiel (Ez 1:10). The eagle was attributed to John by the Church Father Hieronymus.  
The slender figure in an elegant, balanced posture with one foot forward is wrapped in a decorative cloak. The cloak, running from the left shoulder around the right hip opens into a mighty relief train that fills the space between the book and a pedestal on the right, the outline of the figure thus appearing compact. Schweigl ornamented the soft surface of the statue with folds and incisions in the hem of the cloak. The soulful face corresponds with traditional representations of St. John the Evangelist, his fine facial features off-set with locks of wavy hair. The visual effect of the sculpture is enhanced by the treatment of its surfaces: gold plate combined with matt and gloss finishes.  
The artist's development included being apprenticed to his father who came from Tyrol. After studying at the Vienna Academy and following his father's death, Schweigl took over the family workshop in Brno. The workshop, which also functioned as a private art academy, produced sculptures for the whole of Moravia, part of Silesia. A series of sculptures for the Church of St. James was one of Schweigl's first independent commissions. He wrote several manuscripts on art and artists in Moravia intended for pedagogical schools, which laid the foundations of art history research in Moravia.  
In a later phase, Schweigl employed the St. John figure in a statue of the saint for a side altar in Vranov Church near Brno.
6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.short_description: The slender figure in an elegant, balanced posture with one foot placed forward is wrapped in a decorative cloak. It was one of Schweigl’s first independent commissions. His writing on art laid foundations for art history in Moravia and his workshop’s output covered Moravia and parts of Silesia.

6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.method_for_datation: The authorship of Andreas Schweigl is recorded in written sources regarding the contents of the Church of St. James (Brno City Archive).
6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.provenance: Parish Church of St. James, Brno
6cb00351-e32e-5685-bff7-6597c47986b7.obtention: This figure was one of several decorative sculptures for the altars in the municipal Parish Church of St. James, Brno. During Re-Gothicization in 1865, the sculpture along with the rest of the contents, were transferred to the parsonage. It has been museum property since 1947.

6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.name: *Lamentation of Christ*
6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.description:
The canvas dates from the Flemish painter's first trip to Rome (1602), and is contemporaneous with his first Roman commission: the paintings for the Sant' Elena Chapel in the Church of Santa Croce in Gerusalemme.  
The work was probably done for Cardinal Montalto and did not become part of the Borghese collection until 1827.  
The scene shows the Lamentation of Christ according to the Gospels. In the centre of the picture, conforming to the dramatic style typical of Baroque art is the body of Christ in a bold foreshortened position, stretched out on an ancient sarcophagus and surrounded by different characters. Mary supports him with the shroud (in which he is wrapped) while looking to the heavens, where beams of light pierce dark clouds, accentuating the almost nocturnal setting of the subject. John the Evangelist, the young apostle loved by Jesus, stands opposite the elderly Joseph of Arimathea. The right side of the painting shows two female figures: one the pious woman, almost hidden, and Magdalene, in full light, in the act of drying her tears. The high drama of the composition and the richness of the colours perhaps come from the famous *Deposition* that Caravaggio completed for the Church of Santa Maria in Vallicella (1602–1604). The painting nonetheless reveals clear references to Dutch Mannerism, combined in this case with classical models copied by the artist in Rome, with brilliant colours and diagonal compositions taken from Venetian and Emilian painting.
6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.short_description: This work was painted by Rubens during his first stay in Rome (1602). He matched Barocci's colours, the dense brushwork of the late Titian, and the roman statuary and the light and shadow of Caravaggio. The Baroque genius had blended, in an absolutely original way, this tradition with new experimentation.
6e2bb82e-c87a-5f17-ab61-576b19d38127.obtention: The Borghese Collection was acquired by the Italian State in 1902.

702f1ab0-167b-5b57-9f33-ce9e777561cf.name: Amalienburg
702f1ab0-167b-5b57-9f33-ce9e777561cf.description: The exterior of the broad, single-storey construction has a pale pink and white stucco facade. Its architectural centre is the round Hall of Mirrors, which curves towards the otherwise straight garden front and is vaulted by a flattened dome. On its roof, a circular platform with a skilfully forged balustrade served as a shooting stand for the Electress’s   pheasant hunt. Two equally sized wings adjoin to the Hall of Mirrors. They house hunting rooms, resting chambers, a kitchen and other rooms for the court society to enjoy their distractions . The stylistically homogeneous interior decoration of the Amalienburg is attributed to a cohesive concept of construction and décor.
702f1ab0-167b-5b57-9f33-ce9e777561cf.short_description: Located in the Nymphenburg Palace Park, the elegant hunting pavilion was built in the style of a French maison de plaisance and is one of the greatest exponents of its kind, due to its prominent artful interior decoration. Starting in 1734, Charles Albert, Prince-Elector of Bavaria, assigned famous architect, François de Cuvilliés the Elder, to plan and build the Amalienburg for his wife Maria Amalia. The capriccio-like stucco décor of the interior in the late Régence  style is regarded as the magnum opus of Munich court stuccoer Johann Baptist Zimmermann.

702f1ab0-167b-5b57-9f33-ce9e777561cf.history: During the reign of Charles Albert’s father, Prince-Elector Maximilian Emanuel, a garden pavilion existed at the location that would later become the Amalienburg. In 1734, Charles Albert tasked his court artist, François de Cuvilliés the Elder, with the construction of a hunting pavilion for his wife, Maria Amalia of Austria, daughter of Emperor Joseph I. Just five years later, the Amalienburg was completed and decorated with Johann Baptist Zimmermann's stuccowork and ornamental carvings from Johann Joachim Dietrich. The style and decorations of the Amalienburg were supposed to resemble a maison de plaisance, thereby following a trend from France where these hunting and summer estates had come into fashion in the 18th century. In accordance with the new living trend at the time, called "commodité" (intimate rooms and retreats for informal relaxation), they were designed to escape the strict court etiquette and indulge in hunting, celebrating and other kinds of leisure distractions in an intimate setting.

7b582bf3-4e6a-5626-8f57-513177ccb1d0.name: *St. Andrew*
7b582bf3-4e6a-5626-8f57-513177ccb1d0.description:
Figure type and a diagonal X-shaped cross identify the subject of the work as St. Andrew, a fisherman from Galilee and Christ's first disciple. The elongated figure, with an S-shaped body and one foot forward, is sketched in light outline. The artist's attention is dedicated to the modelling of body volumes and the rendering of a system of draperies in an elaborate network of parallel and crossing lines of varying density and intensity.  
Josef Winterhalder Sr. came from a family of sculptors in Schwarzwald. After studying at the Vienna Academy he settled in Moravia, in Olomouc and Znojmo. At the beginning of the 1740s, shortly after a trip to Dresden, where he studied sculptures by Balthasar Permoser, he obtained a large commission in Náměšt nad Oslavou. Between 1740 and1744 he created a series of 20 larger-than-life statues of saints and angels in shell limestone for the Náměšt Bridge, one of three of the kind surviving in the Czech Republic. Winterhalder invited the sculptor Alexander Jelínek, member of a renowned family of sculptors from Velké Meziříčí, to collaborate with him. Winterhalder produced several drawings associated with the commission, three of which are preserved in the graphic art collection at the Moravian Gallery. The drawings represent St. Joachim, St. Andrew and St. Michael. Brilliant specimens of Baroque drawings for sculpture they demonstrate the essential part the artist Paul Troger played in shaping Winterhalder's drawing style. Similar drawings have also survived for the decoration of the Dominican Church in Brno.  
The drawings of Josef Winterhalder Sr. significantly contributed to the further dissemination of Paul Troger's influence among artists active in Moravia. Winterhalder employed his drawings, for example, in the training of his nephew, the future painter Josef Winterhalder Jr. Winterhalder's drawings were also used by other artists, such as Johann Lucas Kracker.
7b582bf3-4e6a-5626-8f57-513177ccb1d0.short_description: The drawing refers to the decoration of the bridge in Náměšť nad Oslavou, one of the few of its kind to survive. Josef Winterhalder came from a family of sculptors in Schwarzwald. After studies at the Vienna Academy he settled in Moravia, first in Olomouc and later in Znojmo.
7b582bf3-4e6a-5626-8f57-513177ccb1d0.method_for_datation: The drawing probably comes directly from the estate of Josef Winterhalder Sr. Its style corresponds with the sculptor’s manner of work.
7b582bf3-4e6a-5626-8f57-513177ccb1d0.obtention: The drawing, acquired as early as 1863, is part of a series possibly passed directly from the estates of Josef Winterhalder Sr. and his nephew, painter Josef Winterhalder Jr. In all probability, the series later came into the property of the sculptor Andreas Schweigl and later the archivist Jan Petr Cerroni, Moritz Wilhelm Trapp and Emil Kořistka, all of whom were curators at the Brno museum.

7c825e0b-6d52-58ef-9ec0-9dab6a28d4e6.name: *Sacrifice of Abraham*
7c825e0b-6d52-58ef-9ec0-9dab6a28d4e6.description:
This relatively large, upright rectangular painting depicts Abraham's sacrifice of Isaac as told in the Old Testament story (Genesis 22: 1–19). Omitting the narrative details of the story, the painter shows the moment Abraham is stopped by an angel just as he is about to carry out the divine command to sacrifice his own son, Isaac.  
The prevailing deep, dusky and dark palette along with dense shadows contrast with the lit masses, the dynamic distribution of which reflect the dramatic charge of the moment. The illuminated accents concentrate attention on the diagonally placed body of the victim, Isaac, while Abraham's elderly, worn-out face reveals his inner turmoil and the difficulty he faced in making the decision. The divine intervention of the angel breaks into the composition from the left, in a foreshortened diagonal of the opposite course.  
The picture is one of four works by Benković that Count Franz Lothar von Schönborn, Elector and Archbishop of Mainz and Prince Bishop of Bamberg, commissioned in 1715 while he was refurbishing the family castle in Pommersfelden. A print by Salomon Kleiner of 1728 shows the interior of Castle Schönborn following its re-arrangement of 1715, which is useful to reconstruct the order of the paintings. On the window wall of the middle room were Benković's *Sacrifice of Abraham* and *Hagar and Ishmael*, and on the ceiling the *Sacrifice of Iphigeneia* and *Apollo and Marsius*. Two paintings – *Hagar and Ishmael* and *Iphigeneia* – are on display in Castle Schönborn to this day, but the French military removed *Apollo and Marsius* and the *Sacrifice of Abraham* from the castle in 1801. The *Sacrifice of Abraham* allegedly turned up in a private collection in Rome in 1868, and then in London in 1936; the Association of Friends of the Strossmayer Gallery bought it in 1936.
7c825e0b-6d52-58ef-9ec0-9dab6a28d4e6.short_description: *Sacrifice of Abraham* is one of four compositions commissioned by Federico Benković for the Schönborn family's castle in Pommersfelden. The painter achieves dramatic tension by depicting the very moment at which an angel stops Abraham from sacrificing his son, Isaac, as told in the Old Testament story.
7c825e0b-6d52-58ef-9ec0-9dab6a28d4e6.initial_owner: Lothar Franz von Schönborn (1655–1729), Elector and Archbishop of Mainz and Prince-Bishop of Bamberg
7c825e0b-6d52-58ef-9ec0-9dab6a28d4e6.method_for_datation: Identification of the Zagreb painting was based on written (the inventory of the castle of the Schönborn family in Pommersfelden) and pictorial sources (a print of the interior of Castle Schönborn in Pommersfelden, 1728).
7c825e0b-6d52-58ef-9ec0-9dab6a28d4e6.obtention: The Association of Friends of the Strossmayer Gallery bought the picture in 1936 in London. In 1868, it was allegedly part of a private collection in Rome, and in 1801, the French government requisitioned the painting in the Schönborn family’s castle in Pommersfelden.

81962cf6-88f1-5463-ae37-6690ad61ec3d.name: *Annunciation*
81962cf6-88f1-5463-ae37-6690ad61ec3d.description: The scene takes place in a domestic interior. The composition, based on a neo-Renaissance perspective shows a nearly archaic poverty. The scene opens outward allowing the viewer to feel directly involved in the event. The employment of three different sources of light is very original: the main light source illuminates the figures coming from the foreground. A light is emanating from a dove that symbolizes the Holy Spirit shines from above. A third beam of light shines from a side door. Far from the spectacular luminosity of Tintoretto, this painting employs a poor, nearly severe palette anticipating a naturalism of feeling and research on the human form. It is a careful representation of life typical of the early Baroque period as depicted by artists such as Caravaggio. Keeping in contact with Raphael and Correggio's noble classicism, Ludovico Carracci portrays life in a quotidian tone with a humble, direct and moving religiosity. This seems to reflect the spirit that a great interpreter of the Catholic Reformation, Cardinal Gabriele Paleotti, Archbishop of Bologna from 1566, applied to the visual arts, in his book *Sacred and Profane Images*, published in 1582. The altarpiece stood on a predella, painted by Camillo Procaccini before his departure for Milan (1585–86), which was lost during the Second World War.
81962cf6-88f1-5463-ae37-6690ad61ec3d.short_description: A symbol of the early Counter-reformation in Bologna (more appropriately of the Catholic Reformation) because of its authentic and direct religious feeling. Based on its humble naturalism and its original experiments with light it is one of the paintings from Lombardy and northern Italy which led to the style of Caravaggio.
81962cf6-88f1-5463-ae37-6690ad61ec3d.method_for_datation: The date 1584, hypothesized by the critics on stylistic basis, has been recently confirmed by historical documents about the building of the oratory where the painting was held (Feigenbaum 1990).
81962cf6-88f1-5463-ae37-6690ad61ec3d.provenance: Church of San Giorgio in Poggiale (Bologna), Oratory of the Holy Sacrament
81962cf6-88f1-5463-ae37-6690ad61ec3d.obtention: Commissioned by Giulio Cesare Guerini, a member of the Company of the Holy Sacrament, the painting became property of the Italian Government in 1866. The painting was taken back to the church of San Giorgio in Poggiale.  It was moved to the Pinacoteca shortly before the beginning of Second World War and it is still on show in this museum.

82491e9f-24e6-5380-8457-1657289a939a.name: Cabinet on stand
82491e9f-24e6-5380-8457-1657289a939a.description:
A large cabinet of the aedicule type standing on the base that belongs to it. In the shape of a horizontally oriented rectangle, and given frontal emphasis by its architectural appearance, its decoration of paintings on glass are framed by veneers of expensive woods – black ebony and tortoiseshell – materials that are also employed to build up the architectural decoration. Rosewood veneer covers the sides.  
The central aedicule with twisted pillars and gilt bronze fittings bears a fragmented gable, surmounted with painted fields organised to make up a lunette, and, in the lower zone, the decorative painting conceals a drawer for valuables incorporated into the architectural elements. The remainder of the front maintains rhythm and mobility by the recession of the central surface and projection of the architectural elements.  
The decorative repertoire of the glass, painted in tempera on the reverse, consists of figures and mythological scenes with the “*amour* of the gods” prevailing. There are also scenic views treated in the antique manner. Forms and landscapes in fresh colours immersed in silver and blue create refined tints and subtle tonal shading. The painted scenes are in the manner of Luca Giordano and more or less precisely repeat the iconographic motifs of his repertoire.  
The base is of richly carved and gilded wood constructed from luxurious, symmetrically conceived, front-facing vegetation – fleshy acanthus leaves powerfully mobilised in S-curves, and floral festoons enhanced with a central motif of mascarons, and figures of *putti*. Lion's-paw feet support the base.
82491e9f-24e6-5380-8457-1657289a939a.short_description: A cabinet with the appearance of an architectural façade fitted with drawers for valuables. Richly decorated with painted glass panels framed with ebony and tortoiseshell, it stands on its own luxuriously carved and gilt base. The decorative repertoire of the glass compositions consist of figures, mythological scenes and views treated in the antique manner. The painted scenes are in the style of the Baroque painter, Luca Giordano.

8288d335-c4ea-550c-8988-3466de55dd87.name: *Madonna in Glory with the Patron Saints of Bologna*
8288d335-c4ea-550c-8988-3466de55dd87.description:
This painting was commissioned by the Government of Bologna to thank the Virgin of the Rosary after the end of the plague in 1630. Originally it was used as a standard and carried in an annual procession, commemorating the end of the epidemic. The procession moved from the Palazzo Comunale to the church of St. Dominic and once there the standard was exhibited in the church for three days.  
The great painting follows a strict order. In the middle of the painting are the patron saints of Bologna, Petronius, Dominic, Proculus and Florian with two Jesuits saints, Ignatius of Loyola and Francis Xavier, gathered around Saint Francis. All the saints look thankfully in the direction of the Virgin. The greyish shade of the sky is broken by a rainbow introducing the Madonna, calm and regal, lit by the only warm beam of light in the whole painting. In the lower part the town of Bologna looks desolately grey, depopulated by the plague, with no shades and half tones, the only signs of life are the small figures of the “monatti” collecting the dead bodies.  
The patron saints and the two Jesuits saints are a significant iconographical change, usually the plague was associated with St. Roch and St. Sebastian: the first one because he had plague himself and the second one because the arrows in his body were compared to the plague wounds. The altarpiece has a strong votive meaning, it shows how the people of Bologna had committed themselves to the Virgin and the patron saints and how grateful they were to be alive.
8288d335-c4ea-550c-8988-3466de55dd87.short_description: This is one of the most famous votive pictures of Seventeenth-century Italian painting. It is a model from which many figures have been copied and rearranged. Technically, it represents a new experiment by the painter. Reni painted on silk, a stronger and more durable material. The shining silk pervades the whole painting with silver luminosity.
8288d335-c4ea-550c-8988-3466de55dd87.obtention: Moved to the Pinacoteca from the Palazzo Comunale in the Napoleonic age.

846382be-ca5f-5bdc-b8e9-6f11b341886e.name: Jesuit and University Church of the Virgin Mary of the Snows, Olomouc
846382be-ca5f-5bdc-b8e9-6f11b341886e.description: Both the construction and the interior decoration of the monumental church (53.5 m x 12.5 m x 24.5 m) were largely executed by local builders and artists. It was based on a traditional model, exemplified by the Jesuit church Il Gesú, in Rome. The Chapel of St. Ignatius contains the tomb of Bishop Vilém Prusinovský (d.1572) upon whose invitation the Jesuits came to Olomouc in 1566. The concept of the building follows an unexecuted design by G. P. Tencalla, which, surprisingly, featured an undulating façade. Echoes of this type of architecture can be found in a number of religious buildings in Moravia and Silesia.
846382be-ca5f-5bdc-b8e9-6f11b341886e.short_description: The church came into existence as part of the university, the oldest Jesuit college in Moravia. Both the construction and the interior were largely executed by local builders and artists. Columns in the frontage evoke the Temple of Solomon. The re-erection of the temple heralds the coming of the Saviour, while the Jesuit's trigram *IHS* is set in a cartouche on the portal. The dedication of the church is associated with a story from the life of St. Ignatius of Loyola: the founder of the Jesuit order held his first service in the Sta. Maria Maggiore church (Church of the Virgin Mary of the Snows), Rome.
846382be-ca5f-5bdc-b8e9-6f11b341886e.method_for_datation: Construction started in 1672 and its course is conveyed in the diaries of the Olomouc college rectors. The altarpiece of the high altar is signed and dated, while contracts with the artist, Haringer, and the sculptor, Thomas Berger, are preserved.

846382be-ca5f-5bdc-b8e9-6f11b341886e.history: The church was built on the site of a former Minorite Monastery, part of the oldest Jesuit college in Moravia. The original church was destroyed by the Swedish army but was not restored as it was not big enough. The new church was constructed following the design and a wooden model by M. Klein under the guidance of L. Klöckel. During a visit by Cardinal Aldobrandini, later Pope Clement VIII, or on state visits by emperors, the church could hold as many as 2,500 people. In 1773, when the Jesuit order was dissolved, the complex passed to the local military garrison and served as a warehouse. Today it is once again accommodates the university established in 1576, renowned in the 18th century for its graphic theses, carved in Czech and German (Augsburg) workshops.

86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.name: *St. Augustine*
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.alternate_name: *St. Augustine Stepping On the Head of Heresy*
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.description:
*St. Augustine* furnished the entrance of the *Nossa Senhora* *da* *Graça* Convent in Lisbon ruled by the order of St. Augustine. Built around 1271, important reforms of 1565 followed by others in the 17th and 18th centuries, transformed the convent into one of the most sumptuous in Lisbon. After the earthquake of 1755 the convent collapsed and was rebuilt. The grand Italianate late Baroque painting, *St. Augustine,* was probably a gift from King José I to the friars, given that Lusitano was the king's first official court painter.  
The Saint, dressed in Episcopal robes, is writing while he steps on the head of Heresy. At his side a *putto* encourages some dogs to attack Heresy while another, in the lower part of the painting, is burning heretic books. An allegorical figure of The Church sits at the upper left-hand side as, rendered in dark ochre, it emerges statue-like out of the shadow. On the right-hand side a classical building in daylight sweeps into the background. Behind St. Augustine are ruined monumental columns. The realism, upheld by the depth of the landscape, contrasts with the crowded, chaotic interior of the St. Augustine's *scriptorium*.  
The painting, signed and dated by Vieira Lusitano, emphasises his nomination as *accademico di merito*, an honour bestowed on him in 1727 by the St. Lucas Academy in Rome. No other Portuguese artist had previously received this honour. Lusitano was influenced by Roman, late Baroque and Rococo art; his teachers included Benedetto Lutti (1666–1724) and Francesco Trevisani (1656–1746), a disciple of Carlo Maratta (1625–1713).  
*St. Augustine,* a large-scale geometric composition with calculated asymmetry and movement, has theatrical appeal. Its characters are set among solid architectural components and a naturalistic background. The *putti,* characteristics from the Roman tradition, enable the artist to play with symbolic elements while the sumptuous use of colour: ochre, red, various blues and white; the flesh tones and gold and silver details in the bishop's robes, is also notable. Vieira Lusitano had many sophisticated patrons. He often made use of allegory to introduce complex ideas into the works he was commissioned to paint.
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.short_description: A late Baroque masterpiece influenced by Roman Painting. The scene, a contrast between the crowded, chaotic *scriptorium* of St. Augustine and the open classical cityscape, celebrates the author, bishop and Father of the Church St. Augustine stepping on the head of Heresy.
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.initial_owner: Convent of Nossa Senhora da Graça, Lisbon
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.method_for_datation: Francisco Vieira Lusitano has signed and dated the picture.
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.provenance: Convent of Nossa Senhora da Graça, Lisbon
86b3e2e2-6141-5567-8390-ebba3dc04e2a.obtention: The convent and the order of St Augustine were extinguished and their assets confiscated by the Portuguese state in 1834. This painting was included among the objects that were confiscated and taken to the Fine Arts Academy Museum in Lisbon. When the museum closed, the collection transferred to the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga in Alvor Palace, Lisbon.

8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.name: Console
8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.description: From a base with four round feet springs the console resembling two vine branches, intertwined with vine-leaves and grapes. The carving is powerful as the volumes are full and in the round. The wood is gilded with silver leaf. The table is painted to look like a dark green false marble, with pale green veins. Formerly thought to be a nineteenth-century remake from a Tuscan workshop, today this console is considered an original piece dating to the eighteenth-century. The original provenance is unknown, but it was likely made in Tuscany. The console is part of the furniture of the baroque apartment, on the first floor of the building which was made between 1736 and 1738 for the wedding of Francesco Tozzoni and Carlotta Beroaldi.
8b0ffe7f-502c-57bf-afc8-2a2f22466bfe.short_description: This piece of furniture is very original; the base is made of vine-shoots and grapes realistically intertwined with a strongly naturalistic carving. We don’t know its original provenance. The console is housed in the red living room of the baroque apartment on the first floor of Palazzo Tozzoni, built between 1736 and 1738 for the marriage of Francesco Tozzoni and Carlotta Beroaldi.

8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.name: *Prince Livio Odescalchi*
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.description:
Prince Livio Odescalchi (1652–1713) belonged to the influential Italian Odescalchi family, a family that throughout history produced important bishops, cardinals and Pope Innocent XI.  
Emperor Leopold I Habsburg, in gratitude for the great financial aid granted him by Pope Innocent XI to meet the costs of the war against the Ottoman Turks, named his nephew Livio Duke of Srijem and granted him the Ilok estate as a fief and many other privileges. Livio himself had excelled in the battle to defend Vienna in 1683.  
He was a great collector and decorated his residences with fine artworks. He was also a patron of the arts.  
The marble *Prince Livio Odescalchi* by the Roman sculptor of French origin, Pierre-Etienne Monnot, is an outstanding work with realistic emphasis on individuality. Dramatic tension is achieved through the expression of the head turned to the right, and by the rich drapery enveloping the body falling in heavy semicircular folds.  
Monnot often worked for the Odescalchi family. He was an excellent master with a fine technique and a strong and characteristic expression reminiscent of Bernini.
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.short_description: The marble *Prince Livio Odescalchi* by the Roman sculptor of French origin, Pierre-Etienne Monnot, shows Prince Livio Odescalchi, a member of the influential Italian family that throughout history produced important bishops, cardinals and Pope Innocent XI. The sculpture shows the influence of Bernini. Livio Odescalchi had links to Ilok and Slavonia by way of the deed of gift he received from Leopold I Habsburg, granting him the Ilok estate and surrounding lands and other privileges for merit in wars against the Ottomans.
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.initial_owner: The Odescalchi family, owners of Ilok Manor
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.method_for_datation: Information about the work is due to the research of the Italian art historian, A. Bachi, an expert in Roman Baroque sculpture.
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.provenance: Artworks including *Prince Livio Odescalchi* were moved to the newly formed Ilok City Museum in 1952, which transferred to Odescalchi Manor in 1968.
8c4696e3-5efb-53c9-9b91-0ce041e3c7ce.obtention: Up until World War II, the Odescalchis owned Ilok Manor. As state property, it had several different uses but after refurbishment in 1968, it became a museum and this bust and other objects from the Odescalchi estate became part of the new permanent collection.

8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.name: St. Michael Archangel
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.description:
This statue was made for the library of the convent of St. Michael in the wood, near Bologna, and dates to the last period of Alessandro Algardi’s activity. The sculptor was born in Bologna but mainly worked in Rome after 1625. In the period of the full flourishing of baroque art he became the main interpreter of classicizing sculpture.  
In this bronze group depicting the struggle between St. Michael and the devil, Algardi leaves aside his usual stylistic moderation. The rhythm is frantic and agitated: the angel is tense as he strikes his final blow; the clothes hang to his legs, while his face and breast keep their beauty unchanged. The sculpture is influenced by the painting of the same subject painted by Guido Reni for the Roman church of S. Maria della Concezione. Compared with the airy elegance of the painting the sculpture appears more rhetoric and forced.
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.short_description: This statue was made for the library of the convent of San Michele in Bosco, near Bologna. It dates to the last period of Alessandro Algardi’s activity. The sculptor was born in Bologna, but after 1625 he worked mostly in Rome. The struggle between the archangel and the devil compelled the artist to abandon his usual controlled style. He adopted a more complex and violent rhythm, while continuing to look for ideal elegance and beauty.
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.initial_owner: Convent of St. Michael in the wood
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.method_for_datation: In his *Vite de pittori, scultori et architetti moderni*, published in Rome in 1672, Giovanni Pietro Bellori notes that Algardi made for Taddeo Pepoli, abbot of the convent of St. Michael in the wood, a statue depicting St. Michael Archangel trampling over the Devil. The statue was to be exhibited in the library, financed and promoted by the same abbot.
8d32099b-f01e-5606-a9f3-a813c2600508.obtention: In 1799, when religious orders were suppressed, the Accademia Clementina took care of the statue, once in the library of the convent; in 1871 it was moved to the Museo Civico and since 1985 it has been exhibited in the Museo Civico Medievale.

8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.name: *Patrona Hungariae sending St. Michael to Fight Against the Turks*
8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.description:
In 1739, the Catholic convent in Sopron commissioned Martino Altomonte – a first-generation member of the Austrian High Baroque – to paint a picture for the high altar in St. Michael's Church. He passed the commission onto his son and collaborator, Bartolomeo. The Altomontes, who specialised in large church paintings, historical and triumphal compositions and frescoes, worked in the Italian Baroque tradition. Martino, although of Tyrolean stock, was born in Naples. He used an Italian version of his real name, Hohenberg, and first used his assumed name at the Polish court, where he painted compositions about the hereditary rulers. Later he was active in Vienna. His son, Bartolomeo, was a pupil of Solimena in Naples for two years.  
The vast altarpiece for Sopron echoes one of Francesco Solimena's (d. 1747) most popular creations, the fresco he painted in the San Domenico Maggiore in Naples in 1709. Bartolomeo continued to make use of details from Solimena's repertoire in his other works representing the Holy Trinity, St. Dominic with other saints, and the defeated heretics.  
In this picture, he adapted the subject to meet the wishes of his employers. The Virgin is represented as the patron saint of Hungary (indicated by the Hungarian coat of arms below her right hand), and the defeated are depicted as Turks wearing clothes and arms painted with pedantic accuracy. The impressive multi-coloured altarpiece, painted in the last years of the so-called Balkan campaign, illustrated for the faithful their release from Turkish rule – by then gradually becoming a reality – a notion suggested in the lower part of the picture by a battle scene, in the upper part by celestial rejoicing.
8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.short_description: In 1739, the Catholic convent in Sopron commissioned Martino Altomonte to paint a picture for the high altar in St. Michael's Church. He gave the commission to his son, Bartolomeo. Although this large altarpiece borrows motifs from Bartolomeo's teacher, Francesco Solimena's, painting in Naples the subject matter has a Hungarian actuality.
8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.method_for_datation: Through archive data, the signature and analysis of motifs.
8e118b35-7d1e-5edb-b151-a23f348816c0.obtention: On loan to the Hungarian National Gallery from the Roman Catholic Parish Church, Sopron.

90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.name: *The Kiss of Judas*
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.description:
The sculpture represents a scene from the Gospel of St. Matthew (26:49) when Judas, one of the apostles, marks Christ with a kiss as the man who should be arrested and tried. As in the sculptures featuring Christ parting with Mary in the Heiligenkreuz Monastery Museum, Austria, and in the Bratislava City Museum, Slovakia, in *The Kiss of Judas* Giuliani concentrates – in the encounter of two figures – on the motif of instant motion typical of the work of Giovanni Bernini, a key baroque sculptor. The dramatic subject of Judas's treason is conveyed by means of the medium as a contrast in the approach to both figures: the figure of Christ is self-absorbed, resigned to his fate, characterised by calm gestures and static drapery flowing in large forms, while Judas approaches Christ in an expressively captured haste which the sculptor has portrayed, aside from Judas's step forward, by a dramatic gesture extended into space, as well as by Judas's clothes floating around the body as if blowing in a wind.  
The sculpture is unique, in that no associates or assistants participated in its creation, as was the case with Giuliani's sizeable works.  
Giovanni Giuliani was apprenticed in Venice, and later in Munich under Andreas II Faistenberger. From 1690 he worked in Vienna, particularly for the aristocracy, in Moravia for the Kounics (Slavkov) and many times for the Liechtensteins (Lednice).
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.short_description: The sculpture depicting a dramatic scene of treason from the Gospel of St. Matthew exemplifies a typical baroque motif of instant motion. Giovanni Giuliani was apprenticed in Venice and later in Munich. From 1690 he worked in Vienna, particularly for the aristocracy in Austria and Moravia.
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.method_for_datation: The overall approach to shape in the figures is classic Giuliani. His authorship is confirmed by the execution of the faces as well as by the softly modelled and finely executed drapery of both figures, which complement not only the form but also become major interpretational elements of the content.
90a1aa86-0d15-5967-aec3-c44d24bea557.obtention: The sculpture became part of the museum’s collections before 1962; its provenance is unknown.

92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.name: *Still life with Fruits, Parrots and a White Cockatoo*
92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.description: Jakab Bogdány left his native town, Eperjes (Prešov) in Upper Hungary, at a young age, going first to Vienna and then to Amsterdam where sources mention him in 1684, and where he may have pursued his studies. At any rate, Amsterdam, then the centre of middle-class genres, especially still life, was a perfect school for an artist just starting out. At first he painted flower and fruit pieces, which proved to be a lifelong experience for him, for the effect of the Dutch example remained discernible in this group of works throughout his life. Bogdány moved to London in 1688, and his technical expertise soon earned him fame among the English aristocracy. His most important clients were the royal family themselves. As a sign of both his artistic and social recognition, he gained English citizenship in 1700 and purchased an estate near London. He began to paint animal compositions, mainly exotic birds, designed for above doors or mantelpieces; most of these pictures are still in situ, found in their original settings in private collections in rural England. Influenced by the painter, Melchior de Hondecoeter, an outstanding Dutch master of bird paintings, Bogdány's are actually elegant genre pictures with exotic birds as actors against a background of elegant parks and classical buildings. He studied, and from the point of view of ornithology, accurately depicted, rare and colourful birds in the aviary at Windsor Park, which belonged to one of his main clients, Admiral George Churchill.
92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.short_description: Jakab Bogdány, born in Eperjes (Prešov), completed his studies in the Netherlands and became famous in England, becoming extremely popular with the English aristocracy. He was a master of the artistic form he practiced – still life paintings with birds – and worked for the royal family. The Hungarian state repurchased his splendid still life paintings with birds in the early 20th century.
92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.method_for_datation: The painting is signed and the date defined by stylistic analysis.
92874325-99be-5a7a-bef3-ee0ac0e45efd.obtention: Purchased from an English private collection in 1907; in the Museum of Fine Arts until 1974 and then transferred to the Hungarian National Gallery.

9a245db6-458e-537c-bdb2-df1379eb0317.name: *St. Roch* and *St. Sebastian*
9a245db6-458e-537c-bdb2-df1379eb0317.description:
These splendidly colourful Rococo statues of *St. Roch* and *St. Sebastian* came to the museum from the parish church of Egervár in the county of Zala. The patron of the church, Count Ignác Széchényi, commissioned a new large tabernacle with six carved figures for the high altar of the church, made in around 1730, in 1757. The Széchényi family already had connections with artists in Graz, the area where Philipp Jakob Straub chose to settle and work.  
Both statues are of saints believed to be protectors from the plague, and both express pain and suffering. *St. Roch*, dressed in pilgrim's clothes, turns his eyes heavenward. His lips parted in pain, he points to the wound on his foot. Next to him is the dog that allegedly brought him bread when he was suffering from the plague. Bound to a tree and wounded by arrows, the young martyr, *St. Sebastian*, is resigned to his fate. His head rests on his shoulder and tears drip from his closed eyes. *St. Roch*'s garments flutter in deep folds, providing the contrast of light and shade, while light glides softly on the sensuously beautiful body of *St. Sebastian*.  
The statues are promoted into the vanguard of Rococo sculpture in Hungary by the outstanding quality of modelling, the subtle and reserved colouring and the empathic rendering of emotions.  
Philipp Jakob Straub was born into the Württenberg family of sculptors and moved to Vienna with his brother, Johann Baptist Straub (later court sculptor in Munich), in 1727. Philipp Jakob Straub studied at the Academy of Fine Arts in Vienna from 1730 to 1733, at which time he settled in Graz. In Graz he worked on commissions for the church, the aristocracy and the middle class, both in wood and in stone. On stylistic grounds, research attributes to him an extensive oeuvre in Styria where he introduced the influence of Bavarian Rococo sculpture and the practices of stone sculpture from the court in Vienna.
9a245db6-458e-537c-bdb2-df1379eb0317.short_description: The high altar in the parish church of Egervár (c. 1730) contained tabernacle statues – two of which were *St. Roch* and *St. Sebastian* – and all of which were commissioned from Styria in 1757. Documents relating to count Széchenyi's relationship with the church and the artist helped to confirm the attribution of these works to Philipp Jakob Straub, a member of the South-German Straub family. Straub settled in Graz and brought fine Rococo sculpture to the Transdanubian region.

9a245db6-458e-537c-bdb2-df1379eb0317.method_for_datation: By stylistic analysis and historical documents.

9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.name: *Antependium with the Tribute of Continents and Imperial Countries to the Holy Family*
9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.description: This colourful embroidery was executed as a “needle painting” and is set within an original gilded frame. An eventful scene opens out with a central motif of columned architecture with staircases and balustrades, and adoring female figures. At the bottom left, four girls kneel, with the coats of arms of the imperial Electors of the clergy who facilitated the foundation of the Franciscan Convent of St. Joseph in Brno. The Archbishops of Treves, Cologne and Mainz are represented by the coats of arms of Karel Kaspar von der Leyen (1652–1676), Maximilian Heinrich von Bayern (1650–1688) and Johann Philipp von Schönborn (1647–1673). Opposite, four girls kneel with the coats of arms of the imperial countries: Bavaria, Saxony, Brandenburg and Pfalz. In the centre are four female personifications of the continents, Asia, America, Africa and Europe, in precious attire. The women and a host of lay people of both sexes pay tribute to the Holy Family. The Virgin Mary is supervising the education of Jesus, while St. Joseph hands to the Pope – a personification of the Church – a sheet with the text *Ecclesiae Petenti Satisfiat*. The scene is crowned with the dove of the Holy Spirit. At the sides are monumental summerhouses with decorative vases and cartouches with the inscription *Ite ad Joseph* (Go to Joseph), while the Old Testament quotation (Gen 41:55) relates to the figure of St. Joseph of Nazareth. In combination with the text on the donated sheet, it elucidates the subject of the embroidered antependium emphasising the role of St. Joseph, patron saint of the Franciscan Convent of St. Joseph in Brno, as a righteous protector of the church and promoter of Divine will. Towards the horizon, various landscapes alternate on the antependium, valleys and hills dotted with dominant castles. The intricate layout of the embroidery may refer to a major event in the history of the Franciscan convent or it could commemorate the establishment and construction of the Convent Church of St. Joseph in 1651–1653.
9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.short_description: The subject of the technically and artistically remarkable antependium is derived from the legends of St. Joseph, a popular saint of the Baroque period. It is one of only a few examples of the use of figurative embroidery in sacred art during the first half of the 18th century, and a specimen of monastery art.
9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.type: Embroidery and painting in original gilded frame
9af64071-595d-57de-a710-92c27227476c.owner: Czech-Moravian Province of the Roman Union of the Order of St. Ursula, Prague (OSU Prague)
